I'll look at the nav user component and the auth provider to see how the picture and email are available today.

You do not need Zustand. `NavUser` already renders an avatar from `user.avatar` and falls back to the first two letters of the email. The sidebar is just feeding it placeholders.

```88:93:web/src/components/layout/sidebar.tsx
        <NavUser
          user={{
            email: "test@test.com",
            avatar: "https://github.com/shadcn.png",
          }}
        />
```

The real values are already on the session. Google and GitHub put them on the Firebase ID token, and `signInIdentity` maps them to `email` and `image` (`token.picture`). `getServerUser()` returns that identity. The same fields are copied into Firestore at login, so you do not need another read just to paint the sidebar.

`AuthProvider` is only a side effect today. It listens with `onIdTokenChanged`, sends the token to `/api/login`, and throws the user away. It does not expose email or `photoURL` to anything else.

Pass them in from the dashboard layout. That layout is a server component, and `AppSidebar` can take props even though it is a client component:

```tsx
const user = await getServerUser();

<AppSidebar
  user={{
    email: user?.identity.email ?? "",
    avatar: user?.identity.image ?? "",
  }}
/>
```

Then hand that same object to `NavUser`. Only render `AvatarImage` when `avatar` is non-empty, so an account with no photo shows the initials instead of a broken image request.

Zustand is the wrong place for this. `useWorkspace` is for dashboard state that changes while you are on the page. Email and photo are identity, they already live on the session cookie, and they do not change without a new sign-in. A store would be a second copy you have to keep in sync with Firebase.

Use `AuthProvider` as React context only if some client component outside this layout needs the same user without a server parent. In the listener you already have, keep `{ email, photoURL, displayName }` from the Firebase user and read it with a `useAuthUser()` hook. The sidebar would then flash empty until that listener runs. The server prop does not.

The server and the client are talking, and that boundary is fine. The dashboard layout stays on the server, reads the session, and passes two plain strings into the sidebar. A client component can take those props. It cannot call `getServerUser` itself.

`getServerUser()` already returns `identity.email` and `identity.image` (the Google or GitHub photo on the ID token). The layout now passes them in:

```18:23:web/src/app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx
      <AppSidebar
        user={{
          email: user?.identity.email ?? "",
          avatar: user?.identity.image ?? "",
        }}
      />
```

`AppSidebar` forwards that object to `NavUser`, which shows the photo when there is one and the email initials when there is not. The image tag uses `referrerPolicy="no-referrer"` so Google profile URLs do not get blocked.

Refresh the dashboard you already have open. The footer should show your email and photo instead of the placeholder.

content.text:
`AuthCta` does not check the session itself. The home page does, once, and passes a boolean down.

`HomePage` is a server component, so it can call `getServerUser()` the same way the dashboard layout does. A user object means they are signed in.

```10:18:web/src/components/home/home-page.tsx
export async function HomePage() {
  const signedIn = Boolean(await getServerUser());

  return (
    <>
      <SiteHeader signedIn={signedIn} />
      <main>
        <HeroSection signedIn={signedIn} />
```

That flag goes to the header, the hero, and the bottom CTA. `AuthCta` only uses it to pick the label and the link: "Go to dashboard" and `/dashboard` when it is true, otherwise the signed-out label and `/auth`.

The marketing page loads with "Meet your agent" when there is no session. Refresh it while you are signed in and those three buttons should say "Go to dashboard".
